# Good morning. Here is today's Korean economic news briefing.

We're starting this Monday, May fourth with a comprehensive look at Korea's economic landscape, where consumer resilience is defying external pressures even as inflation concerns mount. Let me walk you through the major stories shaping our economy today.

## Consumer Strength Amid Global Uncertainty

Our first major story reveals an encouraging sign for the Korean economy. Despite ongoing geopolitical tensions in the Middle East, consumer spending has reached its highest level in twenty-three quarters. This is a remarkable achievement considering the external headwinds we're facing. Household consumption is proving to be a stabilizing force in our economy, showing that domestic demand remains robust even when global conditions are uncertain.

However, analysts are cautioning that downside risks still loom on the horizon. The sustainability of this consumption boom depends heavily on whether inflation remains manageable and employment stays strong. The fact that consumers are spending confidently suggests they believe their job security and income growth will continue, but any sudden shock could reverse this positive momentum.

## Currency Markets and the Carry Trade Effect

Moving into our financial markets section, we're seeing an interesting dynamic develop in currency trading. The interest rate differential between Korea and other major economies, particularly the United States, has created what analysts call the "won carry trade." This is becoming an increasingly important factor influencing exchange rates.

The dynamics are straightforward: when interest rate gaps widen, investors borrow in low-rate currencies and invest in higher-rate ones. This puts pressure on our won and affects export competitiveness. As the Federal Reserve maintains its hawkish stance—having held rates steady at three point five to three point seven five percent with several dissenting voices—the rate differential becomes even more pronounced. This is something Korean policymakers are monitoring closely as it affects everything from corporate profitability to consumer import prices.

## Virtual Asset Taxation Coming into Focus

The government is now moving forward with cryptocurrency taxation plans that have been a hot topic in the investment community. Starting in 2027, virtual asset gains will face a twenty-two percent separate capital gains tax. The National Tax Service is already beginning system preparations for mandatory reporting that will begin in May 2028.

This is significant because it marks the end of the tax exemption that has allowed cryptocurrency investors to operate without specific taxation on their gains. The industry is expressing concerns about potential discrimination against domestic exchanges, and there's debate about whether losses should also be factored into taxation calculations. Meanwhile, there's also discussion about the so-called near-ground tax that collects sixty-nine trillion won annually, which some argue creates an unfair burden on wage earners whose incomes rise but taxable bases remain static. The national tax revenue as a proportion of total government revenue has reached historic highs, raising questions about the overall tax burden.

## Automotive Sector Shifts

In a historic development for Korea's automotive industry, Kia is poised to surpass Hyundai in domestic monthly sales for the first time since the group's integration in 1998. This represents a significant shift in the market dynamics between the two affiliated companies. Industry analysts attribute this partly to supply chain issues affecting Hyundai, including a major component supplier fire and Palisade model recalls that have disrupted production schedules. Kia's strong performance demonstrates the competitive nature of Korea's automotive sector and shows that market share can shift rapidly based on operational efficiency and product availability.

## Energy Price Pressures

Adding to inflationary concerns, LPG prices have surged eleven percent in May alone, with propane costs rising one hundred forty won per kilogram in just one month. This sharp increase reflects the prolonged Middle East conflict's impact on global energy prices. The government has attempted to absorb some of these cost increases to maintain price stability for consumers, but the underlying upward pressure remains significant.

## Macroeconomic Outlook and Growth Revisions

The Bank of Korea is expected to hold rates steady at their May monetary policy meeting, despite growing inflation variables. Interestingly, multiple international investment banks have simultaneously raised Korea's growth forecast within the past month. Current expectations center on 2.7 percent growth for this year, reflecting strong first-quarter GDP performance of 1.7 percent quarter-over-quarter and ongoing strength in semiconductor exports driven by the AI super-cycle.

However, inflation expectations have also been revised upward. As oil and currency movements from Middle East tensions fully feed into consumer prices, we're likely to see significant increases in the inflation rate. The Bank of Korea's March consumer price index stood at 118.80, representing 2.2 percent growth year-over-year, but May figures are expected to show acceleration.

## Stock Market Boom and Leverage Concerns

The KOSPI index has become the story of April, rising thirty point six one percent over the month and repeatedly hitting all-time highs, approaching the 6750 level. This explosive rally has created interesting dynamics in derivatives markets. Inverse leveraged ETF and ETN products designed to profit from market declines are now facing potential delisting as their underlying thesis—that the market will fall—becomes increasingly untenable.

On the other hand, companies are issuing zero-coupon convertible bonds at unprecedented levels, raising one point one trillion won over the past six months. This reflects the conviction among major corporations that share prices will continue rising, making these debt instruments attractive as equity substitutes.

## Virtual Asset and Battery Sector Developments

The battery industry is experiencing a transformation as electric vehicle demand cools. Energy storage systems, or ESS, are becoming an increasingly important revenue driver as AI data centers require massive power storage infrastructure. This is allowing Korean battery makers to diversify away from the slowing EV market and improve their profitability outlook.

The government is also investing heavily in sovereign AI capabilities, with the National Growth Fund directing five hundred sixty billion won to AI company Upstage for local language model development. This investment underscores the government's commitment to establishing technological independence in critical AI infrastructure.

## Real Estate and Policy Debates

In real estate news, the debate over housing policy is intensifying as Seoul's competitive mayor race approaches. While Seoul's overall apartment prices have remained relatively flat, some areas like Songpa-gu and Seocho-gu are showing signs of recovery, with buyers returning after a period of pessimism. Meanwhile, in Gyeonggi Province surrounding Seoul, rental prices are surging as renters migrate from the capital, with rental inventory down thirty-two percent since the beginning of the year.

## International Trade Tensions

Finally, the global trade environment is deteriorating. President Trump has announced a tariff increase on EU automobiles from fifteen to twenty-five percent, effective next week, in what appears to be retaliation for Europe's insufficient cooperation regarding Iran policies. Germany alone faces projected losses of fifty-two trillion won from this action. Korean automakers are watching carefully to see if similar pressure will be applied to their exports.

## Summary for Investors and Viewers

The overarching picture for the Korean economy shows resilience in consumption and manufacturing, supported by the semiconductor and AI sectors. However, inflation is rising due to geopolitical factors, the Federal Reserve's hawkish stance is pressuring the won, and new taxation on virtual assets is coming. For investors, the stock market rally has been extraordinary, but leverage in financial products creates tail risks. For everyday citizens, expect higher energy and import-related prices in the coming months, though wage growth and employment strength provide some cushion. Keep monitoring the Federal Reserve's next moves and Middle East developments, as these will significantly influence our economy's trajectory.

That concludes today's economic briefing. Thank you for your attention.
